project.title: Residential Energy Forecasting Under Changing Conditions
project.short_description: A leakage safe, pre-registered study of how forecasting models, input choices, retraining policies and prediction intervals hold up when a house moves from winter into spring. It forecasts household electricity use 10 minutes, 1 hour and 1 day ahead, and reads a frozen 33-day test period exactly once.
project.overview:
Household electricity forecasts drive demand response schedules, battery control and anomaly alerts. A forecast that looks good in a random train/test split can still fail in real use, because a deployed system predicts the future from the past while conditions change. This project uses one house from the UCI Appliances Energy dataset (10-minute readings over 137 days). I froze an evaluation protocol before training anything, selected models on earlier weeks only, and then read the final 33 days exactly once. That single test read audits four decisions under the same seasonal drift:

  • model vs simple baselines
  • which inputs to use
  • whether to retrain
  • whether prediction intervals stay calibrated

The results include the expectations that turned out wrong, all with paired confidence intervals.
project.problem_statement:
The public study that released this dataset predicts energy use at the same moment from simultaneous sensors. That is a regression, not a forecast. Real deployments must forecast ahead using only past information, and they face drift: it gets warmer, routines change, sensors move. The research question was: when a house moves from winter into spring, which of the usual forecasting choices still hold up?

  1. Do learned models beat simple baselines?
  2. Do extra inputs (indoor sensors, weather) help beyond the house’s own consumption history?
  3. Does retraining (weekly, daily or drift-triggered) improve accuracy?
  4. Do prediction intervals stay calibrated under drift?
project.dataset_info:
• Source: UCI Appliances Energy Prediction (dataset id 374). One low energy house in Belgium, 19,735 readings every 10 minutes from 11 Jan to 27 May 2016.
  • Target: Appliances, energy use in Watt per 10 minutes. It’s typically 50–100, with sharp spikes.
  • Features available: 9 indoor temperature/humidity sensors, lights, an on-site outdoor sensor, and airport weather (temperature, pressure, humidity, wind, visibility, dew point).
  • Leakage finding: the airport weather columns are interpolated between hourly readings, so a value at 17:10 already encodes the 18:00 reading. Features use only the last real hourly observation.
  • Chronological splits:
    • Development: 11 Jan–22 Apr, with 4 rolling-origin folds of 14 day blocks
    • Embargo: 23–24 Apr
    • Final test: 25 Apr–27 May (33 days), read once
  • The drift: mean outdoor temperature over the previous 24 hours averaged 5.9 °C in development and 12.0 °C in the test period.
  • Licence: CC BY 4.0. The raw file isn’t re-hosted because the weather data is third-party; it’s downloaded and checked against a SHA-256 hash.
project.methodology:
1. Task: forecast Appliances 10 minutes, 1 hour and 1 day ahead, using only information available at forecast time. Primary metric: mean absolute error (MAE).
  2. Input sets:
    • A: own recent consumption plus time of day and weekday
    • B: A plus lights and indoor sensors
    • C: B plus airport weather and the outdoor sensor
    • N: C plus two random columns, as a negative control
  3. Forecasters:
    • 6 baselines: persistence, last hour mean, same time yesterday, same time last week, time of day profile, time of week profile
    • Learned models: Ridge, random forest and LightGBM, with small frozen grids chosen on development folds only
  4. Retraining policies: frozen, weekly, weekly on a 28 day window, drift-triggered, and daily.
  5. 80% prediction intervals: raw quantiles, conformal calibrated once, recalibrated daily, and adaptive conformal (ACI).
  6. Drift monitor: a model independent classifier that compares the last 7 days of inputs with the 28 days before. It triggers retraining at AUC ≥ 0.65.
  7. Statistics: day block bootstrap (5,000 resamples) with paired 95% CIs, plus Bonferroni adjusted CIs for the three headline comparisons. A difference counts as supported only if its CI excludes zero.
  8. Discipline:
    • The protocol was frozen on a pinned git branch before any model ran.
    • The model selection was frozen on a second branch before the test was read.
    • A ledger records the one-time test access with the commit, protocol hash and data hash.
project.implementation_details:
• Library (src/energyshift): data loading and boundaries, leakage safe features, baselines, models, retraining policies, interval methods, drift monitor and bootstrap statistics.
  • Scripts: data download with checksum, development grid and selection, the one time final run, post hoc diagnostics, and figure and report generation.
  • Leakage tests: one unit test corrupts every row after the forecast time and requires identical features. A second test proves the first can fail.
  • Testing: 43 automated tests covering leakage, split boundaries, label availability, bootstrap coverage, and interval and policy logic.
  • Size: about 2,200 lines of Python. The development grid takes about 1 hour on 2 CPU cores.
  • Negative controls passed: the random columns got at most 1.0% of model importance, and a model trained on shuffled targets never beat the baseline (error ratio 1.02–1.19).
  • Audit trail: three logged deviations, including a fix to the drift monitor’s windows made before any test data was read.
project.results:
• Models beat baselines at every horizon, but the gain shrinks with distance. LightGBM using only the house’s own history beat the best baseline by 15%, 11% and 3% at 10 min, 1 hour and 1 day ahead. In MAE: 22.1 vs 26.1, 33.1 vs 37.3, and 36.8 vs 37.9 Wh. All paired CIs exclude zero.
  • Extra inputs never helped, and weather hurt badly a day ahead. At one day ahead, adding weather inputs added 12.8 Wh of error (+34%). Validation had warned of only +0.9 Wh. A post hoc breakdown points to the inputs whose values moved furthest outside the training range: airport weather (+12.3 Wh) and the outdoor sensor (+10.4 Wh).
  • Retraining mattered little. Only at 10 minutes did it help in a supported way (about 1% of the error). The drift triggered policy retrained 3 times for −0.22 Wh, against −0.26 Wh for 33 daily retrains. At 1 hour and 1 day, no policy’s CI excluded zero.
  • Intervals were already calibrated. Raw quantile intervals covered 80–82% of outcomes against a nominal 80%, so recalibration made little difference. Adaptive conformal was worse at one day ahead: 78% coverage with intervals about 21% wider.
  • The drift was a step, not a slow change. A cold first week (5.7 °C) was followed by weeks near 14 °C. The drift monitor fired from 7 to 16 May but didn’t track daily error (Spearman −0.16, CI −0.52 to 0.23).
  • Pre-registered hypotheses:
    • H1 (models beat baselines only at longer horizons): partly wrong, since they beat it at all three, including 10 min.
    • H2 (weather adds little): right, and understated.
    • H3 (retraining helps modestly): supported only at 10 min.
    • H4 (raw intervals under-cover under drift): wrong.
project.future_improvements:
• Repeat the audit on a second house or dataset to test whether the input group finding transfers.
  • Add an input range guard that falls back to the own history model when inputs leave the training range.
  • Replace past weather observations with weather forecasts.
  • Diagnose why adaptive interval calibration got worse at one day ahead.
  • Add a holiday calendar and a spike oriented probabilistic model.
project.my_role:
I designed and carried out the study end to end:

  • reformulating the dataset as a true forecasting task and finding a leakage problem in its weather columns
  • writing and freezing the protocol before any model ran
  • building the features, baselines, models, retraining policies, interval methods and drift monitor
  • writing the leakage and boundary tests
  • running development selection and the one time final evaluation
  • analysing the results and publishing the README, figures and project page
project.key_learnings:
• How easily leakage hides in a dataset: interpolated weather columns quietly encode the future, and only a deliberate audit and a test that corrupts future rows catch it.
  • Why time-series evaluation must be chronological, with an embargo and a test period read once, rather than random splits.
  • That validation can miss failures under distribution shift. Inputs that look harmless in validation can break a forecast once conditions leave the training range.
  • How to compare choices with paired day block bootstrap intervals, and how to report hypotheses that turned out wrong.
  • Practical conformal prediction, adaptive conformal inference and drift detection with a domain classifier, including their limits.
  • Running a study with pre-registration, frozen git branches and an access ledger.

related.title: Plant Disease Classifier Reliability Study
related.short_description: A pre-registered, leakage-audited study testing whether plant disease classifiers that score ~99% on PlantVillage stay reliable on field style PlantDoc photos, and whether their confidence can be trusted to say “I don’t know.” It compares a scratch CNN with a fine-tuned ResNet-18 across three seeds.
